Let
\[
u=\log x,\qquad g(u)=f(e^u).
\]
Then \(u>0\), and the three quantities become
\[
A=\frac1u\int_0^u g(s)\,ds,\quad
B=\frac2{u^2}\int_0^u (u-s)g(s)\,ds,\quad
C=\frac3{u^3}\int_0^u (u-s)^2g(s)\,ds.
\]
Writing \(D=u\frac{d}{du}\), differentiating gives
\[
DB=2(A-B),\qquad DC=3(B-C),\qquad DA=g-A.
\]
Hence
\[
B=C+\frac{DC}{3},\qquad
A=C+\frac56DC+\frac16D^2C.
\]

Set
\[
y=2-C.
\]
The given identity becomes
\[
y+\frac32Dy+\frac12D^2y=y(y+Dy).
\]
Equivalently, if
\[
z=y+Dy=(uy)',
\]
then
\[
Dz=2(y-1)z.
\]
Now \(C(e)=3/2\) means \(y(1)=1/2\), and the limit condition is
\[
\lim_{u\to\infty}uy(u)=1.
\]
Since \(uy\) rises from \(1/2\) to \(1\), we must have \(z>0\). Put
\[
p=\frac zy.
\]
Then
\[
Dy=y(p-1),\qquad Dp=p(2y-1-p).
\]
So for \(q=p-y\),
\[
Dq=-(1+p)q.
\]
Thus the sign of \(q\) is fixed. The comparison solution with \(q=0\) satisfies
\[
Dy=y(y-1),\qquad y(1)=\frac12,
\]
so
\[
y(u)=\frac1{1+u}.
\]
If \(q>0\), then \(y/(1+u)^{-1}\) increases from \(1\), forcing \(\lim uy>1\). If \(q<0\), it decreases from \(1\), forcing \(\lim uy<1\). Since the limit is exactly \(1\), we must have \(q=0\), hence
\[
C(u)=2-\frac1{1+u}.
\]

Now recover \(g\). Since
\[
A=C+\frac56DC+\frac16D^2C
\]
and \(g=A+DA\), substituting \(C=2-y\), \(y=(1+u)^{-1}\), gives
\[
g(u)=2-y^4=2-\frac1{(1+u)^4}.
\]
Finally \(u=\log x\), so

\[
\boxed{f(x)=2-\frac{1}{(1+\log x)^4}}.
\]
